business_problem: Bristol Myers Squibb needed to scale AI across global research and clinical development, but fragmented data, isolated teams, and rising computational demand made it difficult to reuse knowledge and deliver faster high-conviction decisions across the R&D pipeline.
solution_summary: Bristol Myers Squibb created an AI factory and center of excellence on NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD to give scientists a shared environment for target identification, molecule design, imaging, clinical-data analysis, and foundation-model development. The platform links research sites so experimental readouts in one location can be reused by teams elsewhere, and it integrates NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit so biological and agentic AI workflows can span multiple programs instead of remaining trapped in local silos. NVIDIA MONAI supports medical-imaging workloads, while NVIDIA AI Enterprise provides the governed production software foundation. BMS is now expanding the system with a second DGX SuperPOD powered by DGX Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and intends to unify both clusters into one globally accessible environment, turning compute infrastructure into a cumulative learning loop for R&D instead of a collection of project-specific resources.

data_flow: Biological, chemical, imaging, and clinical data from multiple BMS programs flow into the shared AI factory, the DGX SuperPOD environment trains and serves models for target identification and molecule design, and agentic workflows reuse the resulting insights across sites and therapeutic areas.
business_outcome: BMS reported 55% overall cost savings, up to 10x higher performance per megawatt than its previous infrastructure, weeks of manual work saved in target identification, and AI-assisted expansion of its CELMoD compound library that is uncovering new targets and potential medicines.
